The convergence of a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) to a function f(x) on [0, 1] does not necessarily imply uniform convergence.

To see this, consider the sequence of polynomials B_n(x) = x^n. This sequence converges pointwise to the function f(x) = 0 on [0, 1). However, it does not converge uniformly on [0, 1).

The reason is that the sequence B_n(x) = x^n does not satisfy the Cauchy criterion for uniform convergence. Specifically, for any ε > 0, there exists an N such that for all n, m > N, |B_n(x) - B_m(x)| > ε for some x in [0, 1). This is because the sequence x^n grows without bound as x approaches 1, so there is no single N that works for all x in [0, 1).

In fact, the sequence B_n(x) = x^n converges uniformly to 0 on [0, 1) but not on [0, 1]. This is an example of a sequence that converges pointwise but not uniformly.

Therefore, the convergence of a sequence of polynomials B_n(x) to a function f(x) on [0, 1] does not necessarily imply uniform convergence.
